author: John Wagner
title: From near death to new life through transplant - NewsBreak
text:
By John Wagner ,
5 hours ago
Tim Born, of North Branch, has always been a positive person.
“Even after I was diagnosed, it didn’t make me lay down and be depressed and mope around,” he said. “If you knew me, you wouldn’t have known that anything was bothering me.
“I always say that my sky is always blue.”
But Born’s diagnosis could have left anyone singing the blues: In 2010 he was diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a rare liver disease where scarring and narrowing of bile ducts leads to liver damage.
Over time, the liver loses its ability to filter blood and support digestion. The only solution? A kidney transplant.
April is National Donate Life Month, which was created by Donate Life America and its partners to raise awareness about the critical need for organ, eye, and tissue donations.
It’s an event that hits home for Born, who received a kidney transplant in February of 2023.
“I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you if somebody didn’t become an organ donor,” Born said. “That’s the main thing that I support.”
Darkness closes in
When Born was diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), he was told that he would need a transplant in 10 to 15 years.
“I made a big mistake and researched what PSC is,” he said. “Everything I read said it’s terminal, and livers are very hard to come by and it’s not good. …
“The hardest thing on me was that [I wondered] when that thing was gonna to kill me. I’m always positive, but I knew I had that bomb in me. When was it gonna go off?”
Born dealt with that fear for 13 years, and that period was far from smooth. Roughly six years after that diagnosis, he started to feel sick; Born said doctors were able to go into his liver and open his bile ducts, which helped him continue to function.
“So I did that once a year for the next however many years,” he said. “I was fine. I felt a little off, but I was functioning. It was not keeping me from doing anything like hunting or fishing or riding a motorcycle.”
That worked until August of 2022, when his hepatologist — a doctor who treats liver diseases, among others — delivered the bad news.
“He said, ‘I’m not gonna sugar coat this: I’m gonna try and get you on the transplant list’,” Born said. “Well, if you have a liver disease, you don’t just automatically get a liver. They tell you right out that there aren’t a lot of livers, and the ones that get transplanted, they have to go to a good home.”
That meant Born had to prove he was a worthy candidate for a transplant, and his ‘worth’ included checking his health, his mental status, his insurance, and a number of other potential issues.
“They wanted to look at just what makes me tick,” he said. “After you go through that, you finally get on the transplant list. You just don’t get on [the list]. That took about three months.”
Then the waiting game began. And while Born was “waiting,” his health continued to decline.
“In three months, I lost 50 pounds,” he said. “I was getting real sick, real fast. My liver was not working properly; all that fluid that it’s supposed to filter, it wasn’t doing it. So all that fluid was ending up in my abdomen.
“So I’d fill up and I’d have to get a paracentesis. That’s where they stick this big needle in your side and they drain out all the fluid. For me, usually they would drain around eight liters of fluid. And they did that once a week. …
“My system was so out of whack, I was freezing to death and then itching. It was just miserable. I might be overreacting, but some nights I thought I was gonna die. … I went out to fill the bird feeder one day, and I fell in the snow. And I could not get up.
“I laid there and sobbed, because it was pathetic.”
Searching for light
That’s when Born started having terrible thoughts.
“I thought, ‘How can I survive this?’ I mean, I was so sick,” he said. “I admit that I thought about making an end-of-life note.”
But Born, a Christian who has been a recovering alcoholic for 39 years, turned to a different source for support.
“I had my notebook out and I was gonna start to write, but instead I said the Serenity Prayer,” he said. “This was at eight o’clock on a Wednesday night. I said that prayer and I just sat there, did nothing. And all of a sudden I just kind of got a burst of energy, just like a fuse lit.
“And I thought, ‘You know what? If I write this note, I’m giving up. And I promised my kids that I wouldn’t.’ I realized that I would get through this. I’ll fight this. I made up my mind: If I write this, I’m giving up. I’m not gonna give up. …
“You hear about people who they say they ‘died peacefully.’ I said, ‘I’m going out kicking and screaming. I’m not going peacefully’.”
Less than an hour after making that decision, Born got a phone call from the University of Minnesota transplant team. There was an older gentleman on life support, and Born was offered his liver.
Success, right? Well, perhaps not.
“The doctors told me that they didn’t want to get my hopes up too high, because a lot of times it doesn’t work,” Born said about the procedure to transplant the kidney. “Sometimes when they look at the kidney, it’s not usable or it doesn’t fit or your body rejects it.”
Born was prepped for surgery on a Thursday, but the kidney didn’t even arrive at the hospital until Friday. That’s when a new complication arose, as his blood type did not match the donor, which meant Born needed plasma to make the transplant work. …
“Finally, just before they wheeled me into surgery, I kissed my wife and said, ‘If I don’t make it, I’ll see you on the other side’.”
To say the surgery was a success would be an understatement. Born said people told him his appearance improved immediately.
“I just bounced back so fast,” he said. “I wasn’t even in the ICU for a full day. I didn’t have a breathing tube. I didn’t have a feeding tube.
“Yeah, I had 14 IVs in me and I was beat up, and I had 39 staples. But I couldn’t have been happier because that bomb that was in me ticking for 13 years was gone.”
The surgery was finished on Friday, Feb. 24, 2023. By the following Tuesday, he left the hospital. The typical hospital stay for a kidney transplant is 10 days.
Soon after that, Born had second thoughts about joining a transplant support group.
“They told me about it pre-transplant, and I wish I would have gone to that,” he said. “It would have been so much better because I would have been told that I was going to make it. … At the time, I just stuck my head in the sand. Let me die in peace. I didn’t want to deal with it.
“But then after I got transplanted, I went on that support group. Now it’s people like me saying to other people, ‘Hang in there, this works, you can do it.’ So I’ve been very active in that.”
That group meets once a week via Zoom and once a month in person. And Born said the stories are inspiring and uplifting.
Light from others
“We have one girl, we call her ‘Drive-Through Michelle’,” Born said. “Some of these people have been on the transplant list for years. Michelle didn’t feel good, so she went to the doctor thinking she had an eye infection.
“The doctor told her that her liver quit working — and in five days, she got a liver transplant. That’s why we call her ‘Drive-Through,’ because she didn’t go through any of this stuff for months.”
Born also told the story about a organ recipient who was placed in a medical coma.
“They put her in a coma for two months because she went into cardiac arrest right after transplant,” Born said. “But she survived it. That’s what we’ve all got in common: we survived it.
“That’s a bond. You go and you get to meet these people and you just have so much in common.
While the health of everyone in the support group has improved following the transplant, Born said it is more impressive that the transplants have also positively affected their outlook on life.
“You don’t hear anybody complain about anything,” he said. “They’re just have a zest for life.”
Meanwhile, Born’s life following the transplant has continued to improve quickly.
“When I came home from the hospital, I was taking 25 different medications, plus a shot twice a day, and having lab work done twice a week,” he said. “In a matter of six months, I was down to just a couple medications. My system adjusted.
“Now I have lab work once every three months. The anti-rejection medicine was I think 18 milligrams a day when I first went home, and now it’s three milligrams a day. If the doctor said I’ve gotta have my hernia fixed, that’s nothing. I’ll bend over and have it fixed.”
On a more serious note, Born has nothing but thanks for the man who donated his liver so Born could live.
“I don’t know another thing about him other than he was a 63-year-old guy, his liver was good, and he died from a stroke,” Born said. “We’ve written letters to the family through LifeSource, telling them we’re so very sorry for your loss, but we wanna thank them for the gift of life.
“That’s all you can do. Some people will hear back from the families, but a lot don’t. I’m gonna keep writing those letters of thanks.”
One obvious lesson Born has learned from this is to not take his health for granted.
“You have to appreciate it and be thankful, because it can change real fast,” he said. “I’ve done that from Day One. I know how to play, to enjoy life to the fullest. ...
“And I was given a gift from somebody, and I respect that, and it’s like I’m borrowing it. So I’m gonna try and take as good of care of my health as I can. And I’m gonna try and be as nice as I can, and have as much fun as I can, out of respect for the donor.
“I think, whoever it was [that gave me his liver] is maybe watching me. What’s my liver doing today?”
Sharing the light
For others who may be dealing with a health issue that requires a transplant, Born strongly recommends the volunteer support group.
“We don’t give medical advice: All we do is share with what happened to us,” he said. “We tell people to talk to their transplant coordinator. … When you get assigned a transplant coordinator, you call them up and say, ‘Hey, I got this problem.’ And they’ll help take care of it for you.
“And the support group, there are some transplant people who’ve been in it for 10 years, and we’ve had a couple of people in our group that are on their second liver transplant. … I concentrate on the pre-transplant people because they are so scared. I tell them I got through it, and I hope it gives them hope. …
“You’re not alone; there’s other people that are going through just exactly what you did. And that’s comfort in its own, especially for the pre-transplant. You see them yellow and sick and scared, and they get transplanted. Now they’re bright, they’re happy. You watch them as they get sicker and sicker, and then all of a sudden they get transplanted and they’re on the other side.”
Born said he has a number of people to thank for his new-found health after the transplant, a list that begins with his wife of 50 years, Linda.
“I also thank God, my donor, and the staff at the University of Minnesota,” Born said. “And I thank everyone who signs up to be an organ donor.”
That organ donation that saved Born’s life is the reason he can maintain his positive attitude.
“What color is my sky today? It’s always blue,” he said. “My sky is always bright blue and the sun is out.”
To learn more about LifeSource and organ donations, go to https://www.life-source.org .
To sign up to become an organ donor, go to https://www.organdonor.gov/sign-up .
For resources to help you work through suicidal thoughts, text or call 9-8-8 or go to https://988lifeline.org/.
